title: Governance Indicator Stability: Do Labs Change Their Safety Documentation After an Index Publication?

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if labs systematically update documentation on low-scoring indicators after being scored, this demonstrates that index scores measure gaming ability rather than safety posture. This is a direct, actionable finding for index design.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: using web archives to compare document versions before and after specific dates is accessible. Coding whether changes concentrate on low-scoring indicators is straightforward analysis.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: two time points (before/after index publication), specific indicators to check, clear comparison methodology. Bounded by the number of labs and indicators.

novelty.reasoning: The FLI AI Safety Index has been published three times (2024, Winter 2025, Summer 2025), providing the necessary temporal data points. While the Index reports note that some labs have improved transparency (e.g., OpenAI publishing its whistleblowing policy after media pressure, Anthropic filling out the survey), no systematic study uses web archives to measure whether documentation changes concentrate on low-scoring indicators — the Goodhart's Law hypothesis. The Stanford Foundation Model Transparency Index shows transparency actually declined (58/100 to 40/100), suggesting the gaming hypothesis is untested. This specific research design — before/after comparison on indicator-specific documentation — is novel.

evidence: FLI AI Safety Index (2024, Winter 2025, Summer 2025). Future of Life Institute.
Stanford Foundation Model Transparency Index (2024-2025) — transparency declining.
Model Alignment: Flaws in the FLI AI Safety Index 2024 (Sedona, 2024)
